---
title: "Research"
---

My research asks how bioactive peptides and their receptors evolve and how they control physiology. I am particularly interested the cases of molecular mimicry, where one organism can control the physiology of its target. I combine fieldwork, comparative genomics, computational biology, and physiological testing to trace the origins and diversification of diverse molecular systems.

## Venom evolution

Venoms have evolved independently across many animal lineages, often recruiting molecules that originally served other physiological roles. In cone snails, I study how a venom system with hundreds of toxins arises and diversifies, and how it responds to ecological change.

Key questions I investigate:

- Where do toxins come from, and why are some proteins repeatedly recruited into venom?
- How do shifts in ecology, e.g. diet, reshape venom composition?
- How do gene duplication, regulatory change, and sequence evolution contribute to evolutionary innovation?

Our work has for instance shown that [prey shifts drive venom evolution in cone snails](publications.qmd) and have traced many cone snail toxins back to ancestral neuropeptides and hormones. My current work at the University of Oslo uses comparative genomics to investigate the origin and loss of venom across marine snails.

[Explore the venom evolution projects →](projects/venom-evolution.qmd)

## Evolution of peptide signaling

Peptide hormones and neuropeptides are ancient, diverse signaling molecules found in multicellular organism from animals to plants. Their evolutionary histories show how communication systems originate, expand, and acquire new functions across animal lineages.

Key questions I investigate:

- How old are the major families of peptide-encoding genes?
- How do duplication and loss shape the diversity of signaling systems, from cnidarians to bilaterians?
- How can toxins and evolutionary analyses guide the discovery of previously unknown peptide ligands?

I began this work with genome-wide surveys of neuropeptide genes in cnidarians and placozoans. More recently, I have used the toxins of cone snails to reconstruct the origins of the somatostatin and allatostatin-C, and to build a toxin-based approach to neuropeptide discovery. We are also developing machine-learning methods to predict neuropeptide precursors from protein sequences.

[Explore the peptide signaling project →](projects/peptide-signaling.qmd)


## Molecular mimicry and host manipulation

Organisms can manipulate one another by producing molecules that imitate endogenous signaling peptides. We call these molecules *doppelgänger peptides*. They are found in venoms, parasites, and pathogens, and they let one species hijack the signaling pathways of another. 

Key questions I investigate:

- How often do interacting organisms evolve molecular mimics, and in which lineages?
- What evolutionary processes allow a mimic to activate a host receptor?
- How do mimics help animals paralyze, defend against, or manipulate other organisms?
- Can comparative genomics reveal the origins and spread of mimicry?

Examples from our work include somatostatin and insulin mimics that disrupt blood glucose in the prey of a fish-hunting cone snail, neurotensin mimics produced by intestinal hookworms, and bradykinin mimics that evolved repeatedly as defensive toxins. We reviewed the field in *Trends in Biochemical Sciences* and *General and Comparative Endocrinology*.

[Explore the molecular mimicry project →](projects/molecular-mimicry.qmd)

## From evolution to application

Toxins and mimics have been refined by evolution to act on specific receptors, which makes them useful starting points for drug discovery. We are working on several potential drug leads inspired by nature.
